Dear all,

I am trying to run a path model with nested data. The data has 10 schools (clusters) and 3-19 students per school, and 128 cases in total. I used the lavaan.survey function. It is to test the relationship among two IVs (Clos, Conf), one mediator (quan), and DVs (CRVT measured at Time 1 and 2). Thus, I tested two mediation paths. Three covariates (A5, gender, and A18) were controlled on each variable. Here is my R script

# ##model specification, with auto-regressor controlled

model1<-'

Clos~A5+gender+A18

Conf~ A5+gender+A18

##Use 'lavaan' function to run analysis.

fit1.clust <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=fit1, survey.design=school_clust)

summary(fit1.clust,fit.measures=TRUE,standardized=TRUE,rsquare=TRUE)

parts: The data has 10 schools (clusters) and 3-19 students per school

Some of the standard errors may not be trustworthy.  Some of the observed covariances or means are collinear, and this has generated collinearity in your parameter estimates.  This may be a sample size issue, missing data problem, or due to having too few clusters relative to the number of parameters. Problem encountered in group(s) 1

Is group 1 the one with only 3 students?  The lavaan.survey package uses the survey package to estimate the within-cluster covariance matrix per cluster, which are then pooled for analysis in lavaan.  In very small clusters, I expect it is quite easy to have correlations of exactly 1.  But your syntax also includes gender, which I assume is a dummy code?  Its variance is therefore its mean (e.g., proportion male) times 1 minus its mean:  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution
Do you see the warning when you remove gender (or any other binary variables)?  If that is the source, you can ignore it, although your analysis model could label its mean (e.g., mg) and its variance (e.g., vg) to constrain its variance to vg == mg*(1 - mg)
But you would still see the warning from survey because that happens when estimating the saturated model.

lavaan.survey just works with the lavaan object you give it, but lavaan's MLM estimator does require meanstructure=TRUE.   By default in single-group, single-level models, lavaan leaves meanstructure=FALSE, so when you run the initial model that you pass to lavaan.survey(), you should set meanstructure=TRUE, so that they are estimated.
 
fitHKCRVT1_1<-lavaan(modelHKCRVT1_1, data=data1, meanstructure=TRUE)

You can notice this was not necessary in the ?lavaan.survey help-page examples because other arguments changed the default anyway (e.g., a multigroup model or setting estimator = "MLM"), but one of the examples does set meanstructure=TRUE anyway.

I am not sure Terrence had explained it anywhere in the thread, but either with the lavaan.svy or with the clustered standard errors, the variance-covariance matrix of the estimated coefficients only has a rank of 10 (the number of clusters). You are estimating 33 parameters. The check that the variance of the estimates is of full rank is a common ad-hoc test for identification (if the model is not identified, it usually manifests in the flat ridges of the likelihood and hence zero eigenvalues); I would argue that it is not appropriate for the clustered standard errors / survey setting -- the check should be on the Hessian matrix, not on the resulting variance matrix as the latter is computed from different principles. This ad hoc test came from the idealistic 1970s world of the i.i.d. data and maximum likelihood where the variance-covariance matrix is the inverse Hessian. That's a deep conceptual issue for Yves (and Dan?) to look into.

I am not sure Terrence had explained it anywhere in the thread, but either with the lavaan.svy or with the clustered standard errors, the variance-covariance matrix of the estimated coefficients only has a rank of 10 (the number of clusters). You are estimating 33 parameters. The check that the variance of the estimates is of full rank is a common ad-hoc test for identification (if the model is not identified, it usually manifests in the flat ridges of the likelihood and hence zero eigenvalues); I would argue that it is not appropriate for the clustered standard errors / survey setting -- the check should be on the Hessian matrix, not on the resulting variance matrix as the latter is computed from different principles. This ad hoc test came from the idealistic 1970s world of the i.i.d. data and maximum likelihood where the variance-covariance matrix is the inverse Hessian. That's a deep conceptual issue for Yves (and Dan?) to look into.
